saint.name: St. Padre Pio of Pietrelcina
saint.summary: When red marks appeared on the palms of a young priest in a southern Italian village, he asked his parish priest to pray that Jesus would take them away. He was willing to suffer, he said, but all of it in hiding. Instead Padre Pio carried bleeding wounds in his hands, feet, and side for fifty years. Doctors argued over them, the Holy Office silenced him, and pilgrims lined up before dawn to hear his Mass and confess to him. Asked how his humility survived it all, he laughed and talked about a gold watch. How did a man who wanted only to be a poor friar who prays carry such a gift without making it his own?
saint.biography:
Neither Mad Nor a Thief

John McCaffery, a friend who visited San Giovanni Rotondo often, once passed on to Padre Pio something he had heard from a Jesuit superior. The Jesuit had been told about the crowds that surrounded the old friar, and he had wondered aloud how anyone’s humility could survive them.

Padre Pio laughed. He laughed harder than McCaffery had ever seen him laugh, as if it were the best joke he had heard in his life. When he could speak again, he gave his friend a message to take back. He hoped, he said, that he was neither mad nor a thief, because a man who claimed for himself what belonged to God alone would have to be one or the other. Then he put it in a picture. Suppose someone handed you a fine gold watch to take to Milan for repair. And suppose that on the train you took it out and showed it to the other passengers as if it were your own. What would that make you? A fool, or something worse.

The watch he meant had been in his keeping for a long time. For fifty years Padre Pio bore wounds in his hands, his feet, and his side, the places where Christ was wounded on the Cross, and they bled. Doctors examined them and disagreed about what they were. A bishop sent by the Holy Office in Rome questioned him in his own friary. The Holy Office declared that nothing supernatural had been proved, and later, for two years, it forbade him to say Mass in public or to hear confessions. People said he could read their souls, that he had been seen in two places at once, and that a scent like violets hung in the air around him. And still they came, to a friary on the Gargano in the south of Italy, until by the time he died his prayer groups counted some sixty-eight thousand members in fifteen countries.

He had not wanted any of it to be seen. The first red marks appeared on his palms while he was a young priest living at home in his village. He asked the parish priest to pray with him that Jesus would take them away. He was willing to suffer, he is remembered to have said, even to die of suffering, “ma tutto nel nascondimento”: but all of it in hiding. What he wanted to be, he said, was only “un povero frate che prega,” a poor friar who prays.

The Catholic Church declared him a saint in 2002, and the pope who did it had knelt at his confessional as a young priest. Padre Pio wrote no books. He said Mass, he heard confessions, he wrote letters to his spiritual directors because they told him to, and in his later years he built a hospital. He asked to suffer in hiding, and he lived half a century in the open, under the eyes of crowds, doctors, and Vatican investigators. How he did it without once showing the watch as his own is the story of his life. It begins in a village in the province of Benevento, with a shepherd boy who thought that every child saw what he saw.

The Boy Who Thought Everyone Saw

In Pietrelcina the neighbors had a name for the Forgione family. They called them the God-is-everything people. In that village the bell of the castle church rang not for the hour but for prayer. The Forgiones went to Mass every day, and every evening the family knelt together for the rosary. Three days a week they gave up meat in honor of Our Lady of Mount Carmel. Grazio Forgione and his wife, Maria Giuseppa De Nunzio, could neither read nor write. They knew the Scriptures by heart all the same, as their own parents had, and they told their children the stories of the Bible.

They were peasants who owned their land outside the village. Of their children, two died as infants. Francesco was born on 25 May 1887 and baptized the next day in the church of Sant’Anna; his mother, who had a great love for St. Francis, chose his name. He grew up with an older brother, Michele, and three younger sisters, Felicita, Pellegrina, and Grazia, who would one day become a nun. He did not go to school regularly, because there was work to do on the land, and until he was about ten his work was minding the sheep.

The people who later wrote about his childhood recorded something stranger. From about the age of five, by his own later account, he saw the Virgin Mary and the Sacred Heart of Jesus come to the altar rail of the village church, Santa Maria degli Angeli. It did not strike him as unusual. He assumed that all children saw the same things. At five, too, he is said to have solemnly given himself to Jesus, and when he played, he played at church.

At ten he came down with typhoid and recovered. That same year, 1897, a Capuchin friar came through Pietrelcina begging for his friary, Fra Camillo of Sant’Elia a Pianisi. The boy told his parents what he wanted to be: a friar, he said, with a beard. It was not a cheap wish. A friar needed schooling that a shepherd boy did not have, so Grazio went to America to work, and the money he sent home paid for a tutor. At twelve Francesco began lessons with a priest, Domenico Tizzani, who took him through the whole elementary course in two years. On 27 September 1899 he was confirmed and made his first Communion, both on the same day, from the hands of the Archbishop of Benevento. When he finally applied to the Capuchins in 1902, they turned him down. That autumn they changed their minds.

He was fifteen when the time came to leave. On New Year’s Day 1903 he received Communion and, as he later told it, was shown that his whole life would be a struggle with Satan. On the night of 5 January, his last at home, he saw God and the Virgin Mary encouraging him. The next day he set out for the friary at Morcone. The Church that declared him a saint sets one sentence of his at the head of his official life, and it reads like a summary of everything that lay ahead:

“The Lord showed me, as in a mirror, that my whole future life would be nothing but a martyrdom.”

“Il Signore mi fece vedere, come in uno specchio, tutta la mia vita futura non essere altro che un martirio.”

— Padre Pio, quoted at the head of his biography by the Dicastery for the Causes of Saints (our translation)

On 6 January 1903 he entered the Capuchin novitiate. Within two years, the body that was supposed to carry him through that life began to fail.

A Novice Who Could Not Eat

On 22 January 1903, at Morcone, Francesco Forgione put on the Capuchin habit and received a new name, Fra Pio, after the pope-saint Pius, the patron of Pietrelcina. A year later he made his first vows, and then the order moved him from one house of studies to the next: Sant’Elia a Pianisi, San Marco la Catola, Serracapriola. One of his teachers was Father Agostino of San Marco in Lamis, who would later be his spiritual director. Looking back, Agostino summed up his student in four words: “buono, obbediente, studioso, sebbene malaticcio.” Good, obedient, studious, though sickly.

The last word was an understatement. From about 1904 his health gave way in one form after another. He lost his appetite, he fainted, he vomited, and he suffered from headaches and bronchitis; for long stretches he could digest little but milk and cheese. At Serracapriola he meditated on the Passion of Christ and wept over it so much that his eyes became diseased. On Good Friday 1908 an illness of the chest came on top of his migraines. To his parents he wrote lightly about the summer heat: “qui si sta un po’ male,” things are a bit hard here, “non v’impensierite,” don’t worry. The friars did worry. Alarmed that he still could not eat, they sent a telegram to his father through the parish priest of Pietrelcina, and Grazio came and took his son home on a doctor’s advice.

On 27 January 1907 he had bound himself to the order for life with solemn vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience. By then he was rarely well. Half a century later a pope would release him from one of the three, so that he could run a hospital.

Illness did not keep him from the altar. He was ordained a deacon at Morcone on 18 July 1909, and on 10 August 1910, in the chapel of the cathedral at Benevento, Archbishop Paolo Schinosi ordained him a priest. He was twenty-three, a year short of the age the Church’s law then required, and an exception was made for him. Four days later he celebrated his first solemn Mass in the church of Our Lady of the Angels in Pietrelcina, where he had seen what he thought every child saw. Because of his health, his superiors let him go on living at home in the habit. For most of the next six years he stayed there, saying Mass in the village and writing to his directors at San Marco in Lamis.

Out at a place called Piana Romana, not far from the village, his brother Michele had built him a little hut. After Mass the young priest would go out there to pray and meditate in the open air, which was good for his weak lungs. It was there, he later said, that something began to happen to his hands.

Red Marks the Size of a Coin

The date he later gave was 7 September 1910, less than a month after his ordination. On that afternoon at Piana Romana, marks appeared in the young priest’s hands. For a year he put nothing about them in writing. When he finally told his spiritual director, in September 1911, he said the marks had been there for almost a year, and he admitted that he had kept quiet out of “that cursed shame.” Then he described what he had found:

“In the middle of the palms of my hands a little red has appeared, about the size of a cent coin, with a strong, sharp pain.”

“In mezzo al palmo delle mani è apparso un po’ di rosso, grande quanto la forma di un centesimo, accompagnato da un forte e acuto dolore.”

— Padre Pio, letter to his spiritual director, September 1911 (our translation)

He also confided in the parish priest of Pietrelcina, Don Salvatore Pannullo, the same priest through whom the telegram had come that brought him home. The village knew him as Zi’ Tore, Uncle Tore. The words Padre Pio is remembered to have said to him run through the rest of this story. “Zi’ Tore, fatemi la carità, chiediamo a Gesù che mi tolga questa confusione.” Uncle Tore, do me this kindness: let us ask Jesus to take this embarrassment away from me. “Voglio soffrire, morire di sofferenza, ma tutto nel nascondimento.” I want to suffer, to die of suffering, but all of it in hiding.

Don Salvatore promised to help him pray. He did not promise that the prayer would be answered the way the young man hoped. If this was God’s will, he told him, he would have to bend to it.

For a time the prayer seemed to work. The marks faded from sight, and for seven years they stayed hidden, as he had asked. The pain, by his own account, never left. And the struggle that mattered most to him in those years was happening somewhere else, in the long letters he was sending to San Marco in Lamis.

Letters to San Marco in Lamis

In the autumn of 1911 he lay sick in the friary of Venafro. On 28 November Father Agostino rushed into his room and found a man who seemed to be dying. Agostino went to the chapel to pray. When he came back, the dying man was alert and full of joy. It is counted as the first of his documented ecstasies. A friar at Venafro said later that for more than twenty days Padre Pio lived on nothing but Holy Communion.

From December 1911 until February 1916 he lived on sick leave in Pietrelcina, mostly in the house of his brother Michele. His two spiritual directors, Father Agostino and Father Benedetto of San Marco in Lamis, asked him to write to them about his soul, and he obeyed. His letters to them from these years and after now fill the first of the four volumes of his collected correspondence, the Epistolario. He often signed off with a request. “Pregate assai per la mia conversione,” he would write. Pray hard for my conversion.

In these letters a young man tries to put into words what is happening between him and God. He wrote about the Eucharist the way a starving man writes about bread. “Before I receive him I have such hunger and thirst that I nearly die of longing,” he told Father Benedetto. Because he could not keep away, he went on, sometimes he had to go and feed on Christ’s flesh with a fever still on him. Prayer was the other place he met him. As soon as he began to pray, he wrote, his soul gathered itself into a peace that words could not express. All his senses fell still except his hearing, and a great noise around him made no difference. Describing one morning when he felt wholly united with Christ, he reached for a simple image:

“My heart had vanished, like a drop of water that loses itself in the sea.”

“Il mio cuore era scomparso, come una goccia d’acqua che si smarrisce in un mare.”

— Padre Pio, letter to a spiritual director, Epistolario (1995 ed.), 273 (our translation)

Suffering, for him, was the other half of that love. “Gesù mi dice che nell’amore è lui che diletta me; nei dolori, invece, sono io che diletto lui,” he wrote. Jesus tells me that in love it is he who delights me, while in sorrows it is I who delight him. So he could write, “Voglio soffrire. È questa la mia brama.” I want to suffer. This is my longing.

There were also seasons when heaven seemed to shut. “Io cerco Dio, ma dove rinvenirlo?” I look for God, but where am I to find him? In May 1913 he confessed to Father Agostino, with startling frankness, that he had asked Our Lady once again for a grace she had forbidden him to ask for. “This Holy Mother flew into a rage at my daring,” he wrote, and from that day she had withdrawn from him, together with the other heavenly persons. In another letter he wrote, “Una sola cosa mi resta amica: la morte.” Only one thing is still my friend: death. And he fought a temptation that will surprise anyone who knows only the legend of the wonder-working friar. It was the wish to be admired. “Dio mio! che martirio è la tentazione della vanagloria,” he wrote. My God, what a martyrdom the temptation of vainglory is.

What held all of it together was the Cross. In one letter he recorded words that he said Jesus had spoken to him: “Sotto la Croce s’impara ad amare.” Under the Cross one learns to love. Calvary, as he put it, was “il monte dei Santi,” the mountain of the saints. He urged the people he guided to stop fighting and let themselves be carried. “Abbandonatevi pienamente sul cuore divino di Gesù, come un bimbo tra le braccia della madre,” he would tell them. Give yourselves up wholly to the divine heart of Jesus, like a child in its mother’s arms.

Not every line in these early letters may be his own. It has been pointed out that eleven letters he wrote to his directors between 1911 and 1913 reproduce long passages, word for word and without saying so, from the writings of Gemma Galgani. She was an Italian stigmatic who was later declared a saint. For his critics, the borrowing raises the question of how much of his early account of himself he learned from her. It is one of the hard questions about the young Padre Pio, and it is part of his story.

In 1915 Father Agostino decided to ask him directly. He sent three written questions “in the name of Jesus”: when the visions had begun, whether he had received the stigmata, and whether he felt the crowning with thorns and the scourging. At first Padre Pio dodged. In his next letter he answered. The visions had begun not long after his novitiate. The marks had been visible, “especially in one hand,” and when he prayed they had been taken away, but “the very sharp pain did not go,” and it was felt above all on certain days. As for the thorns and the scourging, he suffered them most weeks.

By then he was writing to someone outside the order as well, a noblewoman named Raffaelina Cerase, and their letters of 1914 and 1915 fill the second volume of the Epistolario. To her he wrote that it seemed Jesus had nothing else in hand but to sanctify her soul. She told him she offered her Communion for all priests, above all the bad ones, and asked him to pray for their conversion, and he approved. He was hard on himself as a priest: every minister of the Lord, he wrote, should work for souls without ever admitting weariness, while he, useless to souls, knew himself “troppo bene,” too well. On the feast of the Assumption in 1914 he set out for her, in a few lines, the road he believed every chosen soul must walk. John Paul II quoted them on the day he declared Padre Pio a saint:

“To reach our final end we must follow the divine Head, who leads the chosen soul by no other road than the one he walked himself: the road of self-denial and the Cross.”

“Per arrivare a raggiungere l’ultimo nostro fine bisogna seguire il divin Capo…”

— Padre Pio to Raffaelina Cerase, 15 August 1914, Epistolario II, p. 155 (our translation)

He was still at home in Pietrelcina, ill and writing, when in November 1915 the army called him up.

The Friary on the Gargano

Italy’s army could not keep him for long. Padre Pio was drafted in November 1915 and posted in December to the Medical Corps in Naples, where he was soon sent home on sick leave. Over the next two years he was recalled, examined, and sent home again, more than once. Not until the middle of March 1918 did the army finally discharge him as unfit, with a double bronchial pneumonia.

Meanwhile his superiors had moved him out of Pietrelcina. In February 1916 he went to the friary of Sant’Anna in Foggia, where he went on feeling ill. On the evening of 28 July, Father Paolino of Casacalenda took him up to the small Capuchin friary of Our Lady of Grace at San Giovanni Rotondo, a town on the Gargano. He felt better there. After a week he had to go back to Foggia, because the provincial’s permission was slow in coming. On 13 August he wrote asking to return, because Jesus had assured him he would be better there. On 4 September 1916 the order came. He was sent to San Giovanni Rotondo provisionally. He stayed for fifty-two years.

The friary stood about a mile outside the town, and seven friars lived there. A week after he arrived, Padre Pio wrote to Father Agostino that the community was edifying, and that his inner night of the spirit was growing. In the same envelope the guardian, Father Paolino, slipped a note of his own. Apart only from his inner pains, Paolino wrote, the new friar “potrebbe dirsi veramente felice,” could really be called happy.

His body was another matter. In January 1917 he fell ill with pneumonia and typhoid, and Father Paolino took his temperature. According to Paolino’s later account, the ordinary thermometer burst after reaching 42.5 degrees Celsius, and when he tried a bath thermometer, it read 52. That year the friars who ran the friary’s school for boys hoping to become Capuchins were called up for the war. In the end only two priests were left, Father Paolino and Padre Pio. Padre Pio heard the boys’ confessions, gave them two talks a week, and ate and prayed with them. In the time that remained, he guided a growing circle of people, in person and by letter. In July 1917 he told Father Agostino that he had no time even to rest in the Father’s heart. “Non mi so negare a nessuno,” he explained. I do not know how to say no to anyone.

On the feast of Corpus Christi, 30 May 1918, answering an appeal of Pope Benedict XV, Padre Pio offered himself to God during his Mass for the end of the war. What followed was a state, lasting for some time, that he felt as being imprisoned in hell. Father Paolino, meanwhile, was watching. Between March and September he saw Padre Pio in ecstasy twice and heard him speaking with Jesus and Mary. He came to believe that the young friar could read the hearts of the people who came to him.

On the evening of 5 August 1918 Padre Pio was hearing the boys’ confessions when, he wrote afterward, he was filled with terror at the sight of a heavenly figure. It held something like a very long blade of iron with a sharp point, and fire seemed to come out of the point. The figure drove it into his soul. He told the boy in front of him to leave. “I barely let out a moan,” he wrote. “I felt I was dying.” The pain lasted until the morning of 7 August, and it did not really end:

“I feel in the depths of my soul a wound that is always open, and that makes me cry out in pain without ceasing.”

“Sento nel più intimo dell’anima una ferita che è sempre aperta, che mi fa spasimare assiduamente.”

— Padre Pio to Father Benedetto, August 1918, Epistolario I, p. 1065 (our translation)

Father Benedetto wrote back that 6 August was the feast of the Transfiguration, and that the wound was a sign of God’s love. The mystical tradition has a name for it, a transverberation, the piercing of the soul by divine love. Six weeks later, after his morning Mass, Padre Pio stayed behind in the choir of the friary church to pray.

The Morning in the Choir

Friday, 20 September 1918, was a quiet day at Our Lady of Grace. Father Paolino had gone to San Marco in Lamis, and the brother who went out begging for the friary was away on his rounds, so the house was nearly empty. Padre Pio said his Mass, and at about nine or ten in the morning he stayed behind in the choir to make his thanksgiving.

For a month he told no one what happened there, not even Father Agostino. In the middle of October he wrote to Father Benedetto, asking whether he must say his fiat, his yes to God, as he looked at “that mysterious figure who has wounded me all over.” Benedetto ordered him, under obedience, to tell everything. Padre Pio’s answer, dated 22 October, opens with a cry:

“My God, what confusion and humiliation I feel at having to make known what you have done in this poor creature of yours!”

“Mio Dio, che confusione e che umiliazione io provo nel dover manifestare ciò che tu hai operato in questa tua meschina creatura!”

— Padre Pio to Father Benedetto, 22 October 1918, Epistolario I (our translation)

Then he told it. “It was the morning of the 20th of last month, in the choir, after the celebration of Holy Mass, when a rest came over me, like a sweet sleep.” He saw before him a mysterious figure, like the one of 5 August, and this one’s hands and feet and side were dripping blood. “The sight of him terrifies me,” he wrote, slipping into the present tense as if it were still happening. “I felt I was dying, and I would have died if the Lord had not stepped in to hold up my heart.” When the figure was gone, he found that his own hands, feet, and side had been pierced, and that they were bleeding. Inside him, he wrote, he heard a constant roar, like a waterfall, always pouring out blood. And he asked for mercy: “My God, the punishment is just and your judgment right, but in the end show me mercy.”

In an account he is said to have given soon afterward to a friend from Pietrelcina, Don Peppino Orlando, he added one detail that the letter leaves out. He had dragged himself on hands and knees from the choir to his cell.

He still hoped that prayer would make the wounds disappear, as it had in Pietrelcina, and in the meantime he tried to keep them out of sight. Filomena Ventrella noticed them that same day. He warned the Ventrella sisters: “Guai a voi se lo dite a qualcuno.” Woe to you if you tell anyone. The next day Nina Campanile saw what looked like a burn on his right hand. “Vi siete scottata la mano!” she said. You’ve burned your hand! He put his hands behind his back. When she tried to kiss the wound on his hand, he said: “Se sapessi che umiliazione mi dai!” If you knew what humiliation you give me! That same day the boys of the seminary saw the marks too.

It was Nina who told Father Paolino, eight or ten days later as he remembered it, and Paolino laughed. Then he went to Padre Pio’s cell, walked in without knocking, and saw the wound in the palm of the right hand, and on the back of it, and on the back of the left. He wrote to Father Benedetto. Benedetto did not come. He asked for silence.

Silence was no longer possible. In that same letter of 22 October he asked Benedetto to imagine the torment, which came, he said, almost every day. The wound of his heart, as he called it, was bleeding without stopping, above all from Thursday evening to Saturday. He was dying of the pain, he wrote, and of the shame that came with it. “Temo di morire dissanguato.” I am afraid I will bleed to death. Yet in another letter after the stigmata he could cry out to God, “How sweet and bitter you are together! You wound and you heal.” In December a second blade, a strip of iron, pierced him from low in his heart to below the right shoulder. He covered his hands with mittens. But a priest’s hands are seen every morning at the altar, lifting the Host and the chalice. The young man who had begged in Pietrelcina for everything to stay hidden now carried the signs of the Passion in plain view, and he was thirty-one years old.

Word of the wounded friar spread, and people began to make their way up to San Giovanni Rotondo. So did the doctors.

The Doctors Who Came to Look

One of the first to look carefully was a friar. Father Benedetto, now his provincial superior, came to San Giovanni Rotondo at last and saw for himself. On Ash Wednesday 1919 he wrote to Father Agostino:

“In him there are not marks or prints, but true wounds piercing the hands and the feet… On Friday it is blood… When he says Mass the gift is exposed to the public, because he must hold his hands raised and bare.”

“In lui non sono macchie o impronte, ma vere piaghe perforanti le mani e i piedi… Il venerdì è sangue… quando dice messa il dono è esposto al pubblico, dovendo tenere le mani alzate e nude.”

— Father Benedetto of San Marco in Lamis to Father Agostino, Ash Wednesday 1919 (our translation)

On 15 and 16 May 1919, on the provincial’s orders, Dr. Luigi Romanelli, chief physician of the civil hospital at Barletta, examined the wounds. The lesions on the hands, he wrote, were covered by a reddish-brown membrane, with no bleeding point, no swelling, and no inflammation in the tissue around them. Then he described a test. “I am certain that those wounds are not superficial,” he wrote. Placing the thumb in the palm and the index finger on the back of the hand and pressing, he went on, “one has the exact perception of the void that is there.”

That summer a professor of medical pathology from Rome, Bignami, examined the same wounds. He did not dispute what Romanelli had seen. His explanation was different: the lesions might have begun as a disease of the skin and been completed, perhaps unconsciously, by suggestion, or by a chemical such as tincture of iodine. In October Dr. Giorgio Festa came. In 1920 he took the friar’s temperature twice a day, and later accounts of his report give peaks of about 48 degrees Celsius, far beyond what a body is thought to survive. His report to the Holy Office in 1925 was favorable. The doctors had looked closely, and they could not agree.

In April 1920 came a visitor who did not look at all. Father Agostino Gemelli arrived at the friary and asked to examine the wounds. Padre Pio, with his superiors behind him, asked whether he had written authorization from the Holy Office. For the friar it was a matter of obedience: without an order, he would not uncover the wounds. Gemelli left offended. In a letter he called the whole thing a bluff and the friar hysterical and psychopathic, and he wrote a severe judgment that the wounds fitted the kind of sores a caustic substance would make. He had never examined them. Whether he had come on his own initiative or at the request of a cardinal in Rome, historians still argue.

Outside Italy the news traveled slowly. As late as November 1920, a Catholic paper in Australia, the Southern Cross, told its readers: “That there is a priest in Southern Italy marked with the stigmata is scarcely known at the moment.” The doctors who had examined his wounds, it added, could only say that they could not be explained from a natural standpoint.

The following June the Holy Office sent its own man. Bishop Raffaello Carlo Rossi of Volterra began his secret visitation on 14 June 1921, and his questioning filled the record with a hundred and forty-two answers. The bishop noted a very intense and pleasant fragrance, like violets, whose source he could not find. He also had to weigh an accusation. A witness had testified that Padre Pio had obtained carbolic acid and veratrine. The friar’s explanation was simple: the acid was for sterilizing syringes, and the veratrine was for a joke on the brothers who took snuff. Rossi saw in it simplicity and a playful spirit.

The bishop asked about the stories of bilocation, too. Padre Pio told him that he did not know how it happened, whether it was his mind that was present somewhere else, or some image of him, or his body. Sometimes, he said, he could sense other people’s sins or virtues clearly. He also asked whether the friar would always submit to the authority of the Church. “Sì, Eccellenza,” Padre Pio answered. “Per la Santa Chiesa è lo stesso Dio che parla.” Yes, Excellency. In Holy Church it is God himself who speaks.

On 4 October 1921 Rossi sent the Holy Office his report. The stigmata, he concluded, were a real fact, neither fraud nor the work of the devil, while the many healings people claimed remained unconfirmed. The report went into the files in Rome. It did not decide what happened next, and before long Padre Pio would have to live out the answer he had given the bishop.

The Town That Kept Its Friar

The Holy Office was the Vatican body charged with guarding the faith. It took its first measures against Padre Pio in June 1922. On 31 May 1923 it issued its finding: “non constat de supernaturalitate,” it had not been established that the events surrounding him were supernatural. In mid-June he was ordered to say Mass only in the friary’s private chapel and to stop answering letters. On 5 July the decree was published in L’Osservatore Romano, the Vatican’s newspaper, and papers around the world took it up.

That summer the Rome correspondent of the London Observer described the friar for English readers. “Padre Pio himself lays no claim to miraculous gifts; he is the most modest and simple of men,” he wrote. “His eyes are kind yet piercing; his voice has a peculiar charm.”

San Giovanni Rotondo refused to let him go quietly. On 26 June the townspeople protested, and Padre Pio was allowed back to say Mass in the church. At the end of July an order came to move him to a friary at Ancona. By one writer’s account, when the rumor reached the town the people rose and marched to the friary, and they would not leave until Padre Pio showed himself at a window. Forty local Fascists, the same account says, took turns standing guard so that he could not be taken away in secret. On 17 August the transfer was put off. He stayed where he was, and for the next eight years the decrees kept coming, each one declining to recognize any supernatural cause.

His family had begun to come to him. A wealthy heiress who had become one of his spiritual daughters, Mary Pyle, had a house in San Giovanni Rotondo, and his mother spent Christmas of 1928 there. She died in January 1929, of pneumonia, at San Giovanni Rotondo. His father would live on in Mary Pyle’s house for years.

Then, in 1931, the Holy See took away everything but the altar. He was stripped of every priestly activity except Mass, and that he could say only in private. No crowds, no confessions. He said nothing in public in his own defense. Long before, in a letter, he had told a superior that he acted only to obey: “Opero solamente per ubbidirvi.” Now the sentence was put to the test.

The silence lasted two years. In 1933 Pope Pius XI ordered the restrictions lifted, and on 16 July Padre Pio said Mass in public again. On 25 March 1934 he was allowed to hear men’s confessions, and in May women’s. The decrees themselves, some writers note, were never withdrawn. In 1939 the new pope, Pius XII, encouraged people to go and see him. For the thirty-four years that remained to him, the confessional would take most of his days.

The Line at the Confessional

His day, McCaffery wrote, revolved around the confessional, and for fifty years he sat in it hour after hour. He rose well before four in the morning to prepare for Mass. In the old church he said it at the side altar of St. Francis, and it was slow: McCaffery, who served it seven times, remembered a Latin Mass of about an hour and a half. Once a day, under obedience, he went to the refectory and ate a spoonful of soup or a forkful of spaghetti, rice, or vegetables. What came after the long day, McCaffery wrote, could hardly be called sleep.

The crowds organized themselves around him. In summer, pilgrims began lining up at the church door at two or three in the morning to get close to the altar. Mrs. Ghisleri, on her first visit, took her place there at about half past two. McCaffery found the women who lived at San Giovanni, whom the regulars called the Holy Women, half funny and half exasperating. They skipped the long queue and charged for the front rows when the doors opened, and in the old church they had been known to chain a stool to the altar rail the night before. Poor Mrs. Ghisleri was bowled over in the rush. By 1950 so many people wanted to confess to him that a booking system had to be set up.

He heard confessions for as many as eighteen hours a day, by popular accounts, and one popular estimate puts the total over his life at some six hundred thousand. He did not always make it easy. Pilgrims sometimes met with what looked like harshness, John Paul II said many years later, and almost all of them came back for absolution. The same pope would name him, with the Curé of Ars, among the great confessors of the Church.

Everything in his day led to the altar or away from it. For him the Mass was Calvary itself. He put its worth in a sentence that is often quoted in a looser form. As Don Giuseppe Ruppi of the Voce di Padre Pio gives it, he wrote this:

“The world could even do without the sun, but it cannot do without the Holy Mass.”

“Il mondo potrebbe stare anche senza sole, ma non può stare senza la Santa Messa.”

— Padre Pio, letter, Epistolario III, p. 59, as given in Voce di Padre Pio, December 2025 (our translation)

Those who came to him for guidance he sent toward prayer, again and again. He taught in short sayings that were easy to carry home, and the Church still quotes them:

“In books we look for God; in prayer we find him. Prayer is the key that opens God’s heart.”

“Nei libri cerchiamo Dio, nella preghiera Lo troviamo. La preghiera è la chiave che apre il cuore di Dio.”

— Padre Pio, as quoted in his biography by the Dicastery for the Causes of Saints (our translation)

To his spiritual daughters he wrote about the Cross the way other people write about flowers:

“Keep Jesus crucified in your heart, and all the crosses of the world will seem to you like roses.”

“Tieni nel tuo cuore Gesù crocifisso e tutte le croci del mondo ti sembreranno rose.”

— Padre Pio, letter to a spiritual daughter, Epistolario III, p. 827 (our translation)

Of his own wounds he almost never spoke. Once, when McCaffery sympathized with him, he admitted that the days were not the worst of it. “It is the nights,” he said. If he let himself fall asleep, the pain of the wounds multiplied. When he wrote a few words on prayer cards for visitors, the effort of holding the pen showed in the way his chin jutted with each word, and afterward he laughed at his own “scrawls.”

McCaffery said that what filled his memories of Padre Pio, more than anything else, was humor. To a husband with a talkative wife, Padre Pio offered to take on fifty percent of her if the husband would keep the other fifty. When McCaffery mentioned his old rector, the friar answered in mock horror: “A Rector! God save us from all such!” Bishop Rossi had noticed the same playfulness back in 1921.

A Monk at the Bedside

After 1943 Allied soldiers began to find their way to San Giovanni Rotondo, and American servicemen wrote about him in Catholic papers at home. Some people came because of a story. McCaffery heard one on a train from Bologna to Rome, from a young farmer near Padua who employed some sixty people. Not long after the war, the farmer said, he had been badly hurt in an accident on his farm, and clots had lodged in both his lungs. The new drugs helped for a while. Then the clots came back worse than before, and he understood that he was dying. He prayed that God would let someone closer to Him than he was plead for him. Then he saw a bearded monk at his bedside, who leaned over, put a hand on his chest, smiled, and was gone.

He felt at once that he was cured, and his doctors, to their surprise, confirmed it. He told no one but his mother, for fear of being thought unbalanced. Months later, invited to lunch at a business acquaintance’s house in Padua, he saw a photograph on the wall and froze: it was the monk. His host told him who it was. He took the train south that same evening, and by five the next morning he was in the church at San Giovanni Rotondo for Padre Pio’s Mass. When the friar came out to the altar, the farmer had no doubt left. He made his confession to him that day. At the end of it, Padre Pio asked him, in the most ordinary voice, how his lungs were now.

On another train, bound for Foggia, McCaffery met an American woman who had come all the way from Hawaii to see Padre Pio and was terrified to go through with it. At Foggia a friar stepped off the same train. He was the very man McCaffery had been describing to her, Father Dominic, an American Capuchin who said that Padre Pio had cured him of cancer. The next day she came hunting for McCaffery. Alone in her room, she had noticed a strong perfume, and she had brought none with her. Father Dominic, hearing the hour, said that was just when he had spoken to Padre Pio about her. “Quick off the mark,” he said.

The stories multiplied. Father Dominic believed that Padre Pio had come to his own father’s deathbed in Milwaukee, as the old man had asked. Luigi Orione, a priest who was himself later declared a saint, reported seeing Padre Pio in St. Peter’s Square in Rome, far from his friary. A later book tells of a little Sicilian girl, Gemma di Giorgi, born without pupils in her eyes, whose grandmother brought her to him in 1947. Afterward, the story goes, she could see the sea and a steamboat on it, and Padre Pio told the grandmother that the child could see. Each was told and retold, and the crowds kept growing.

Padre Pio would not explain any of it. Asked about the perfume people noticed around him, he called it “just sweets for the children.” And when the Jesuit wondered about his humility, he talked about a borrowed watch.

In the late 1940s a young Polish priest who was studying in Rome, Karol Wojtyla, came to San Giovanni Rotondo and stayed nearly a week. He went to Padre Pio’s Mass, where he noticed the dark scab that covered the wounds in the friar’s hands, and he made his confession to him. By one account he asked which of the wounds hurt most, and Padre Pio told him it was the one on his shoulder. Wojtyla wrote years later that it was his first meeting with Padre Pio, and that he considered it the most important. A story spread that Padre Pio had foretold the young priest’s election as pope. Cardinal Stickler reported that Wojtyla had told him so, John Paul II’s secretary denied it, and John Paul II himself dismissed the story. By then the friar had already begun the work that would outlast him.

A Home for the Relief of Suffering

In 1925 an old convent in San Giovanni Rotondo was turned into a small clinic with a few beds for the worst cases, and in the late 1930s an earthquake destroyed it. At the end of 1939 Padre Pio began to talk again about a hospital with a small group of men. On the evening of 9 January 1940 each of them put down a small donation, and the friar said that he wanted to give his offering too. He handed over a small Swiss coin that someone had given him that morning. He named the project the Casa Sollievo della Sofferenza, the Home for the Relief of Suffering. “This evening my earthly work has begun,” he is remembered to have said.

Two years later, on 17 February 1942, with Europe at war, Pope Pius XII asked Catholics everywhere to pray for peace. Padre Pio urged his spiritual children to answer by forming groups that would meet to pray together. By one account these were the beginnings of his prayer groups, which other sources date to the 1950s. A bulletin named after the hospital, started in 1949, helped them spread. The hospital and the groups belonged together in his mind: without prayer, he said, the House for the Relief of Suffering would be like a plant without air and sun.

When the builders started in May 1947, they had no architect’s plan and four million lire in the bank. Barbara Ward, a British humanitarian worker, heard one of his Masses, met one of his doctors, and asked that part of UNRRA’s reconstruction fund go to the hospital, and UNRRA granted 325,000 dollars. Through her, McCaffery remembered, a large early gift came in memory of Fiorello La Guardia. And in the pocket of his habit Padre Pio kept a fifty-lira note that a poor widow of the district had offered him. He would take it out and show it, McCaffery remembered, sometimes in tears. The work, he insisted, was not his. It belonged to Providence. If he could, he said, he would have built the hospital in gold.

His father, Grazio, died on 7 October 1946 and did not see it finished. An outpatient clinic opened in 1954. On 5 May 1956, a bright and sunny day, the Casa Sollievo della Sofferenza was dedicated. It had two hundred and fifty beds, two operating theaters, departments from cardiology to obstetrics, and a farm of its own for milk, eggs, poultry, and oil. Gino Ghisleri had searched Italy for its doctors, nurses, and a community of nursing sisters. A seed had been sown, Padre Pio said at the opening. John Paul II later said that he wanted medicine that was warm and human, and that through charity like this God’s “ordinary miracles” take place.

To mark the opening, an international conference of heart specialists met at San Giovanni Rotondo, and Padre Pio received them at the friary. One of them, the heart specialist Paul Dudley White, kept pressing close with his camera as the friar spoke, and on his way out he said, “And, Father, congratulations on your wounds!” McCaffery was in the room too. When his turn came to be introduced, Padre Pio asked him which part of the world he came from. “San Giovanni Rotondo,” McCaffery said, and that afternoon the friar warned McCaffery’s wife, with mock gravity, that her husband had disclaimed his native land.

In 1957 Pius XII dispensed Padre Pio from his vow of poverty so that he could oversee the hospital. The vow that the sickly student had taken half a century earlier now gave way to a building with two hundred and fifty beds. In 1959 he was ill himself, and on 1 July the friary’s new church was consecrated while he was in the hospital. On 6 August a statue of Our Lady of Fatima stopped at San Giovanni Rotondo, and that day, the Vatican’s own chronology records, he recovered. But the hospital’s money brought new suspicion.

Under Suspicion Once Again

Opponents began to allege that the funds were being misused, and worse. In 1960 listening devices were reportedly hidden in Padre Pio’s cell and in his confessional, and in June a Vatican official, Monsignor Pietro Parente, reported on the recordings to Pope John XXIII. Notes the pope wrote on 25 June, published only in 2007 by the historian Sergio Luzzatto, speak of improper relations between the friar and women of his circle, “if what is reported is true.” They also say: “Mi dispiace di P.P. che ha pur un’anima da salvare, e per cui prego intensamente.” I am sorry for P.P., who has a soul to save after all, and for whom I pray intensely. In a later note he called him an idol of straw.

The pope sent Monsignor Carlo Maccari, secretary-general of the Diocese of Rome, to investigate. Maccari met Padre Pio nine times. In his diary he accused the friar of evading his questions with reticence, narrow-mindedness, and lies, and summed up his impression as pitiful. He recommended moving the friars gradually, bringing in an outside superior, limiting each penitent to one confession a month, and writing new statutes for the hospital. A Capuchin writer later told a different story about the tapes. Archbishop Andrea Cesarano of Manfredonia, he wrote, explained to the pope that the kisses on them were his own sister kissing the friar’s hand, and John XXIII lifted his eyes and said, “Sia lodato Dio!” Praise be to God. The guardian of the friary in those years, Father Rosario of Aliminusa, wrote that Padre Pio never once failed in obedience.

In the middle of it all a letter arrived in Latin. It came in November 1962 from Karol Wojtyla, then a bishop in Krakow, who had visited San Giovanni Rotondo as a young priest after the war. He asked Padre Pio to pray for a forty-year-old mother of four daughters who had spent five years in a German concentration camp and was now gravely ill with cancer. Angelo Battisti, a Vatican official who also ran the hospital, drove the letter to San Giovanni Rotondo, and Padre Pio had him read it aloud. “Angelo,” he said, by Battisti’s account, “to this one it is not possible to say no.” He told Battisti to keep the letter, because one day it would be important.

The woman was a doctor named Wanda Półtawska. She was due for surgery, and when the doctors examined her, they found nothing to operate on. On 28 November Wojtyla wrote again to thank Padre Pio: she had been suddenly cured, before the operation. When he telephoned her husband, the man told him that the doctors were facing a mystery.

For Padre Pio himself, the second storm passed more quickly than the first. On 30 July 1964, under Pope Paul VI, he was given back full freedom in his ministry, and his financial affairs were placed under the Holy See. Padre Pio had been only a shareholder in the Casa, and in his will he left it to the Holy See. In 1965 and 1966 he received permission to keep celebrating the old Latin Mass and then to celebrate seated. He moved about in a wheelchair now.

Some time before the end, something else changed. Slowly, the wounds he had carried since 1918 began to disappear.

Have You Said Mass Yet?

In July 1968 Paul VI published the encyclical Humanae Vitae. Padre Pio wrote to the pope to assure him of his obedience and to promise him his prayers and his sufferings. Obedience had been the pattern of his writing from the first letters, which he wrote because he was told to.

On Friday, 20 September, fifty years to the day after the morning in the choir, delegates of the prayer groups gathered at San Giovanni Rotondo from Switzerland, Austria, England, America, India, Brazil, and France. Two days later, at five in the morning on Sunday, 22 September, Padre Pio celebrated Mass for the anniversary. Because of the crowds it was a solemn Mass, and television crews were there. He was eighty-one and very frail. On the altar steps he nearly fell, and the friars had to hold him up.

A writer in Voce di Padre Pio tells a story from the anniversary. A friar said to him, “Cinquant’anni, padre!” Fifty years, Father! And Padre Pio answered, as if his mind were somewhere else, “Cinquantotto, sono cinquantotto.” Fifty-eight. It’s fifty-eight. Count back from 1968 and it comes to 1910, the year of the first marks he remembered, on a young priest’s hands at Piana Romana.

That night Father Pellegrino Funicelli sat up with him. After nine he called Pellegrino on the intercom to ask the time, and Pellegrino saw that his eyes were red from a quiet, gentle weeping. Around midnight, Pellegrino wrote a week later, he seemed like a frightened child, and he asked the friar to stay with him. Then, long before dawn, he asked a strange question. “Have you said Mass yet?” Pellegrino said that he had not. “This morning you will say it for me,” Padre Pio told him.

He asked to make his confession. Afterward he renewed his religious profession, the vows he had made as a young man. He asked Pellegrino to beg the community’s forgiveness for all the trouble he had caused them, and to ask them to pray for his soul. He sent his blessing to his brothers, to his spiritual children, and to the sick. To his niece Pia, to the nephew he called Ettoruccio, and to Sister Pia he sent his love: they knew, he said, how much he had loved them.

At one o’clock he wanted air. The old man who now went everywhere in a wheelchair got up and walked to the friary terrace straight and fast, Pellegrino wrote, like a young man. He sat there for about five minutes, looking around as if he were searching for something. Then he could not get up again. Pellegrino wheeled him back to his cell, and Padre Pio told him to take the wheelchair away. He grew pale, his forehead wet with sweat, his lips turning dark, and he began to repeat, more and more softly, “Gesù, Maria.” Jesus, Mary. When Pellegrino started for the door to fetch help, Padre Pio told him firmly not to wake anyone. Pellegrino went anyway.

Doctors were called from the hospital, and his nephew Mario Pennelli came too. They gave him oxygen. A friar anointed him. At about half past two on the morning of 23 September 1968, Pellegrino wrote, he gently bowed his head on his chest. He died wearing his habit, with his rosary in his hand. Dr. Gusso, one of the doctors at his side, said afterward that it was the most serene passing he had ever witnessed.

The wounds were gone. They had faded gradually before the end. When the doctor at his bedside examined his body, he is said to have found the hands, feet, and side completely healed, without a trace or a scar. His coffin lay in the church while pilgrims filed past it. On 26 September more than a hundred thousand people came to his funeral from all over Italy. The procession wound through the town, and that evening he was buried in the crypt of Our Lady of Grace. Some time before he died, he had allowed a BBC crew to film him at Mass, though not to interview him. Its producer, Mischa Scorer, later told McCaffery that the crew had set one lamp to shine straight onto the altar, and that on the morning of the filming every lamp worked except that one. The documentary was broadcast the following January.

Two Healings and a Pope

The Capuchin order moved quickly to begin his cause. On 29 November 1982 Rome gave its clearance for the cause to begin, and the Archbishop of Manfredonia opened the inquiry in the diocese, which ran from 1983 to 1990. Its work was declared valid on 7 December 1990. In 1997 the Vatican’s theologians and then its cardinals and bishops agreed that he had practiced the Christian virtues to a heroic degree, and on 18 December John Paul II declared him Venerable. The official summary of his virtues noted that he had spent the day and much of the night in conversation with God. He had accepted his superiors’ measures, and the calumnies against him, in silence.

The miracle for his beatification came from Salerno. Between 1 and 6 November 1995, Consiglia De Martino, a woman of that city, was healed of a ruptured thoracic duct without treatment. A church tribunal in Salerno studied the case from 1996 to 1997. On 30 April 1998 the Vatican’s medical board found the cure scientifically inexplicable, without a dissenting vote. The theologians agreed in June, the cardinals and bishops in October, and the decree on the miracle followed on 21 December 1998.

On 2 May 1999, in St. Peter’s Square, John Paul II declared Padre Pio blessed. The Capuchin friar, he said, had “astonished the world.” In his homily he spoke of the friar as someone he had known: “Quando ero studente qui a Roma, ebbi io stesso occasione di conoscerlo personalmente.” When I was a student here in Rome, I had the chance to meet him myself.

He had come back more than once. In 1974, as a cardinal, he said Mass at the tomb. In 1987, as pope, he came for the centenary of Padre Pio’s birth, and spoke to the friars of the man he had known. “Non furono forse l’altare e il confessionale i due poli della sua vita?” he asked them. Were not the altar and the confessional the two poles of his life? In the Mass, he remembered Padre Pio saying, there is the whole of Calvary.

The second miracle happened in San Giovanni Rotondo itself. On 20 January 2000 Matteo Pio Colella, a boy of seven, fell ill with fulminant bacterial meningitis in its septic form, and he recovered. The decree recognizing the miracle followed on 20 December 2001.

On 16 June 2002, again in St. Peter’s Square, John Paul II declared Padre Pio of Pietrelcina a saint. He called him “il Santo Frate del Gargano,” the friar-saint of the Gargano. He said that he too, as a young man, had benefited from the friar’s readiness to hear confessions. And in his homily he let the friar describe himself, in his own words: “Sono un povero frate che prega.” I am a poor friar who prays. The pope quoted another of his sayings too, that prayer is the best weapon we have, a key that opens the heart of God. The Catholic Church keeps his feast on 23 September, the day he died.

Six years later, his tomb was opened.

Why the Crowds Still Come

The exhumation began after midnight on 3 March 2008. Archbishop D’Ambrosio reported that the body was in fair condition: the skull was partly skeletal, but the chin and the body were well preserved, and the hands looked as if they had just been manicured. No sign of the stigmata could be seen. For the public display a silicone mask was made of his face, modeled on a photograph from 1968. On 24 April 2008 Cardinal Saraiva Martins said Mass before about fifteen thousand people as the body was shown. The display was extended until September 2009. In April 2010 his remains were moved to a new crypt decorated in gold.

Popes kept coming. Benedict XVI visited the shrine in 2009, and Francis went to Pietrelcina and San Giovanni Rotondo in 2018. In February 2016, at Francis’s request, Padre Pio’s relics were carried in procession down the Via della Conciliazione into St. Peter’s Basilica, together with the relics of St. Leopold Mandic, for the Jubilee of Mercy. The friar who had spent his life in the confessional lay in St. Peter’s on Ash Wednesday, when that year’s Lent began.

Pietrelcina, by one estimate, now receives about two million pilgrims a year. The prayer groups he encouraged received statutes approved by the Vatican in 1986, and by 2013 there were some 3,300 of them, with about three million members in sixty countries.

Three years after his death, Pope Paul VI tried to explain the fame of this friar to the superiors of the Capuchin order. Padre Pio, he pointed out, had been no philosopher and no scholar, and he had no means of his own. So why had the world come to him?

“He said Mass humbly, he heard confessions from morning to evening… He was a man of prayer and suffering.”

“Diceva la Messa umilmente, confessava dal mattino alla sera… Era un uomo di preghiera e di sofferenza.”

— Pope Paul VI to the Capuchin superiors, 20 February 1971 (our translation)

It was the same answer Padre Pio had given in his own way. As a young priest he had asked the parish priest of Pietrelcina to pray that the marks would be taken from him, and before his death they were. When his tomb was opened forty years later, no sign of a wound could be seen on the hands that had bled for half a century. What remained in San Giovanni Rotondo were the things he had spent the gift on: an altar, a confessional, a hospital, and people who pray. The watch had gone back to its owner.

A Note on the Sources

Padre Pio’s letters are still under copyright, and the printed Epistolario was not read for this account. His words are quoted in short passages, in our own English, from Church documents, the Italian Wikipedia and Wikiquote, and articles in Voce di Padre Pio that cite the letters by page. The letter of 22 October 1918 was read on two Italian websites that agree word for word, though the opening cry is on only one. The lines about the waterfall and the punishment come from Voce di Padre Pio.

In his later account the first marks date to 7 September 1910, and the wounds that stayed to 20 September 1918. The accounts that go back to Padre Pio place that morning in the choir with the friary nearly empty. The Vatican’s obituary of 1968 says instead that a brother found him unconscious behind the high altar. His crawl to his cell rests on an oral account with no named source, and his words to the parish priest come from the Italian Wikipedia without one.

Sources differ on his entry to the novitiate in 1903, his call-up in 1915, the visits of Bignami and Festa, and the restrictions of 1931. They differ on Wojtyla’s visit (1947 or 1948), the day of the last Mass, and when the prayer groups began (1942 or the 1950s). They differ on whether the wounds faded over months or days, and on which pope Pius gave him his name. The Italian Wikipedia dates his answer to Father Agostino’s three questions to 1911, while Voce di Padre Pio dates it to 1915, which we follow.

The last night follows McCaffery and a Spanish translation of Father Pellegrino’s report of 29 September 1968. For the events of 1960, the pharmacist’s story about carbolic acid (which Gaeta and Tornielli call unreliable), the borrowings from Gemma Galgani, and the details of the exhumation we had only encyclopedia and news summaries. The newspaper passages of 1920 and 1923 are quoted as printed in a 2018 article in The Irish Catholic. Accounts found only on one devotional website are left out, as are a remark often attributed to Pius XI and a prayer often attributed to Padre Pio.

How This Life Was Researched

This life draws on thirty-eight sources in Italian, English, and Spanish, one of them seen only in a search summary. They include the official biography and the record of the cause from the Holy See, four homilies and addresses of John Paul II, and the Vatican newspaper’s obituary of 1968. Nine come from Voce di Padre Pio, the publication of the Capuchins of San Giovanni Rotondo, most of them quoting his letters by page. Others are the account of the friar who sat with him on the night he died and the memoir of his friend John McCaffery. A 2018 article prints two newspaper reports from 1920 and 1923. Padre Pio’s own words come from about fifty short passages of his letters and recorded sayings. The positio of his cause, the decrees on his miracles, and the full text of his letters were not read.
